Issued at 135 PM EDT Tue Jul 28 2026

Pattern / Forecast Synopsis: 

Northwest flow regime remains entrenched across the Great Lakes and 
upper Midwest as a robust thermal ridge remains anchored over the 
spine of the Rockies, and troughing holds over northern Quebec into 
the Canadian maritimes. Result will be the continuity of progressive 
flow across the region, bringing quick-hitting periods of shortwave 
trough passages mixed in with height rises and surface high pressure 
passing over the region, though this status quo may face some 
alteration by the conclusion of the forecast period. 

Current short-term trend showcases yesterday's shortwave trough has 
been forced south and east into the eastern Great Lakes, with 
closing off surface low pressure anchored just north of Lake Ontario 
and southwest into northeast Ohio. Attendant cold frontal boundary 
stretches from roughly Toronto south and west through Cleveland and 
into Indianapolis, with cooler and drier air moving into the upper 
Great Lakes, courtesy of an area of surface high pressure and 500mb 
height rises, which will lead to a strong subsidence inversion 
building. Drier air aloft will mix to the surface through the day 
today, eventually scouring out ongoing low level cloud cover. 
Surface high pressure moves overhead into tonight, bringing about 
seasonable temperatures and lower humidity to the region through 
Thursday. Backside return flow manifests by Friday ahead of the next 
progged shortwave trough passage, which should also coincide with 
the next rain chances across the region. At this juncture, potential 
for severe storms looks quite murky given the uncertainty regarding 
timing of the feature's passage. Will have to watch how this 
particular shortwave is forced, as current guidance trends toward 
the ongoing closing-off system over the northeast CONUS to cut off 
and stall over New England, which may turn our upper flow northerly, 
and lead to a chain reaction blocking pattern either by the end of 
or just beyond the forecast period. 

Details: 

Seasonable and dry through at least Thursday: High pressure 
intruding coinciding with 500mb height rises should scour out 
moisture and bring a comfortable, seasonable airmass to the region 
through at least Thursday, perhaps even most of Friday pending the 
passage of the next shortwave. Anticipating a relatively longer run 
of little changing weather conditions in comparison to the observed 
summer thus far. Result will be sunnier days across the region with 
highs in the 70s and 80s both today and Wednesday amid a much less 
humid airmass. This will allow overnight lows to dip into the upper 
40s and mid 50s across the interior through Wednesday night, with 
the coasts holding near 60 degrees. Plume of higher dewpoints creeps 
in by Thursday, leading to a subtle uptick in humidity, though a 
lack of synoptic forcing should put a cap on any convection. 
Southerly flow builds by Friday, bringing even more humid air and 
warmer temperatures ahead of the next approaching system. Highs 
Thursday and Friday peak into the 80-87 degree range, with 
overnight lows generally 55 to 65+ across the board. 

Next Rain Chances: Aforementioned next system builds into the upper 
Midwest come Friday, and should approach the Great Lakes by Friday 
night. Lots of mixed signals with this system considering unknown 
evolution of the system currently over the eastern Lakes into the 
St. Lawrence River Valley. In the event that this ongoing system to 
our east closes off and forces a southerly dig of longwave troughing 
just to our east, this may veer our upper flow more northerly. In 
the event this trend is realized, the next system may deliver 
nothing much more than a glancing blow to the region, as opposed to 
passing right overhead. As such, will be hesitant to go with much 
more than scattered shower and storm activity Friday into Friday 
night, because in the event this does occur, deeper moisture plume 
will be suppressed away from the region and rain chances will 
be confined to our south for the time being. The other caveat 
this presents is that the progressive flow regime we have been 
entrenched in for months now may take a backseat to potential 
blocking in the mid levels... especially considering the jet 
stream will essentially be riding north of the US / Canada 
border, thus limiting any meaningful synoptic mechanisms to 
force and cutoff systems out of any given area. Certainly 
something to watch going forward, with non-zero potential for 
longer lasting, block-dominant weather trends to manifest by the
end of or just beyond the forecast period.
